1o1gxdj:205: The article proposes a simple yet profound improvement-strategy loop: first use Harness engineering to get immediate feedback (add instructions, add tools, adjust orchestration strategies); after hitting an intelligence ceiling, collect training data for fine-tuning; after fine-tuning, use new Harness engineering to explore the boundaries of new model capabilities. The core insight of this sandwich structure is: Harness engineering suits most teams with short feedback cycles and high bandwidth; fine-tuning is a long-feedback-cycle method used after hitting a ceiling. The two are not substitutes but complements — Harness engineering determines where the ceiling is, and fine-tuning pushes the ceiling upward.

1rkx3jn:220: The article’s core formula is: evaluation set = the Agent’s training data. Finding good data + finding a good fitting function = improving the Agent. This perspective unifies all Agent improvement methods (SFT/RL, Harness engineering, memory banks) into a “data integration problem” — the only difference is the target location of integration (weights, configuration, context). This unified framework stops teams from “trying whatever direction is hot” and instead makes data-driven decisions: analyze Traces → discover improvement points → curate evaluation sets → run experiments, forming a measurable, reproducible improvement flywheel.
1snpwx:232: Scaling Dreaming (scaled dream-making) describes the process of integrating Agent data back into the Agent itself across large-scale data and long time spans. The difference between this concept and the traditional “Scaling Law” is that it focuses not on simple growth in model parameters or training data volume, but on how interaction data generated by Agents in real environments is systematically recovered, distilled, and reinjected into the Agent system in a cyclical process. This is a paradigm shift from “passive training” to “active evolution” — Agents are no longer artifacts frozen after a single training run, but systems that continuously learn from their own experience.
